title: Does a square have only one line of symmetry?
description: A square piece of paper is folded straight down, straight across and along both diagonals. Each fold that makes the halves cover each other is counted. Keeko doubts that a diagonal fold can count.
teaching_notes: One idea: a square has a matching fold in four different directions, and each such fold is a line of symmetry. Watch for students who count only the straight folds and leave out the two diagonals.

source: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square piece of paper and, by folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
video_script.why: The child finds every matching fold of a square by trying folds in an orderly way.
video_script.substitution: Fold a square piece of paper down, across and along each diagonal, and see whether the halves cover each other.
video_script.anchor: A square piece of paper that can be folded in four ways
video_script.wrong_answer: the diagonals are not lines of symmetry
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a diagonal cannot be a line of symmetry because it cuts through the corners. Folding along a diagonal makes the two triangles cover each other exactly, so the idea is struck out.
video_script.payoff_line: Every fold that covers exactly is a line of symmetry.

final_answer.value: No; 4 lines: vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals
final_answer.spoken: no, a square has four lines of symmetry, the vertical, the horizontal and the two diagonals

never_show: a count before the folds are made
a tick on a fold before it is tried
maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
A diagonal is a line joining two opposite corners.
A square has four folds that match: down the middle, across the middle, and along each of the two diagonals.
Each of the four folds makes the two halves cover each other exactly.
Slip: believing that a diagonal cannot be a line of symmetry because it passes through the corners.
video_script.design: One idea: find all the matching folds of a square. Assumes the child has seen the fold test for mirror halves. The square stays on the board from the hook to the end.
